{{Short description|Physicist, peace activist}}
{{About|the South African educator and pacifist|the former vice-president of the United States|Mike Pence}}
{{Use British English|date=September 2014}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2026}}

'''Michael John Pentz''' (30 November 1924 – 29 May 1995) was a [[physicist]], activist in the [[peace movement]], and an influential pioneer of teaching science to university students by [[distance education]]. Pentz was born in [[Cape Town]], South Africa, and died in France.<ref name="Dalyell">{{cite news| authorlink=Tam Dalyell| last=Dalyell | first=Tam | title=Obituary: Professor Mike Pentz | url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/obituaryprofessor-mike-pentz-1621848.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220514/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/obituaryprofessor-mike-pentz-1621848.html |archive-date=14 May 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live | newspaper=[[The Independent]] | date=31 May 1995 | accessdate=24 November 2011 }}</ref>

==Life==
Pentz was educated in South Africa at St Aidan's College, [[Grahamstown]], and went on to attend the [[University of Cape Town]]. He came to [[Imperial College]] in London in 1948 to work on microwave spectrometry and nuclear physics. Nine years later he joined [[CERN]]<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pentz |first1=Mike |title=Mike Pentz (sitting, wearing sandals) |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/40181?ln=no |website=CERN Document Server |date=1961 |publisher=CERN PhotoLab |access-date=2 December 2022 |ref=CERN-PHOTO-61074146_b}}</ref> in [[Geneva]], where he was appointed leader of a large group of scientists developing the CESAR accelerator facility.<ref name="Koziol">{{cite web | last=Koziol | first=Heribert | title=On the hunt with CESAR | publisher=[[CERN]] | url=http://public-archive.web.cern.ch/public-archive/en/People/Koziol-en.html | accessdate=17 June 2014 | archive-date=18 March 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140318100759/http://public-archive.web.cern.ch/public-archive/en/People/Koziol-en.html | url-status=dead }}</ref>

Throughout his life, Pentz was a prominent member and activist in a number of highly committed political bodies. In 1965, while working at CERN, he became the first president of the newly founded [[Mouvement Anti-Apartheid Suisse (MAAS)|Mouvement Anti-Apartheid Suisse]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hof |first1=Barbara |last2=Ienna |first2=Gerardo |last3=Turchetti |first3=Simone |date=2024-09-09 |title=The Protest that Never Was: Silencing Political Activism at CERN Before and During the Vietnam War |journal=Physics in Perspective |volume=26 |issue=3–4 |pages=211–236 |language=en |doi=10.1007/s00016-024-00317-6 |issn=1422-6960|doi-access=free |bibcode=2024PhP....26..211H }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Ar 38 Anti-Apartheid Bewegung der Schweiz, Mouvement Anti-Apartheid Suisse |url=https://www.findmittel.ch/archive/archNeu/Ar38.html |access-date=2026-08-28 |website=www.findmittel.ch}}</ref> From 1981 to 1984, he was Vice-Chair of the [[Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament]] (CND). Together with fellow Open University academic [[Steven Rose]], Pentz was instrumental in the movement [[Scientists against Nuclear Arms]] (SANA), which he set up in 1981;<ref name="Dalyell"/> SANA was one of the forerunner organisations of [[Scientists for Global Responsibility]] (SGR).<ref>{{cite web |last1=SGR |title=20 years of Scientists for Global Responsibility |url=https://www.sgr.org.uk/pages/20-years-scientists-global-responsibility |website=SGR |access-date=2 December 2022}}</ref> 

For health reasons, Pentz retired to [[Bonnieux]], near [[Avignon]], in France. He died of [[leukaemia]] in 1995.

==Career==
* Student of physics and electrical engineering at [[University of Cape Town]] earning a BSc (Hons) degree (1944); this was followed by an MSc in physics (1945).
* 1948–49 Research assistant; 1949 assistant lecturer; 1949–57 lecturer, Department of Physics, [[Imperial College London]]
* 1957–58 Research fellow; 1958–68 senior physicist, [[CERN]], Geneva
* 1969–85 Founding dean and director of studies, Faculty of Science, [[Open University]]
* In 1987, the Open University conferred the title emeritus professor onto Pentz.

==Open University==
Since his early days in South Africa, where in 1943 he helped found the Adult African Night Schools Association,<ref name="Rose1">[[Steven Rose|Rose, Steven]]. "The physicist who preached peace", The Guardian, 31 May 1995, Features, p. 14.</ref> to his time at CERN where he threw himself into extramural activities aimed at broadening educational opportunities and spreading scientific knowledge, Pentz had a passionate commitment to the [[public understanding of science]]. In 1969 he was invited by [[Walter Perry]], the first vice-chancellor of the Open University, to become the founding dean and director of studies of the science faculty. He pioneered the teaching of science at a distance, overcoming not only a variety of practical difficulties, but also many prejudices against the notion that science could be taught by correspondence and television. Writing in 2006, Steven Rose<ref name="rose">{{cite news| last=Rose | first=Steven | title=Starting with a piece of liver...and other classic introductions | newspaper=[[Times Higher Education]] | date=15 December 2006 | url=http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/story.asp?storyCode=207206&sectioncode=26 | accessdate=28 July 2012 }}</ref> described the immense challenge:

{{blockquote|The nine of us (two biologists, two chemists, two earth scientists and two physicists, plus our charismatic dean, Pentz) who constituted the initial Open University science faculty back in 1969, shared many commitments as to how and what we wanted to teach. Central was the uncompromising insistence that we were going to teach science, not "about science". In these days of dumbed-down courses and lowered standards, this might read strangely. Our view was that an OU science graduate should be able to compete on level terms with those from any other university when it came to going on to a science-based career, including research. And teaching science meant, above all, lab experience. But how do you achieve this in a distance-learning institution?}}

Led by newest research in [[educational technology]], they overcame the difficulties by developing a multi-media approach, using printed texts, radio and television broadcasts, support from tutors in face-to-face tutorials, residential schools, and by the innovative use of home experiment kits.<ref name="OUvideo">Video clip from the Open University Archive on OpenLearn, The Open University {{cite web |url=http://www.open.edu/openlearn/education/educational-technology-and-practice/educational-technology/1971-home-experiment-kits |title=1971 - Home experiment kits - OpenLearn - Open University |accessdate=2012-06-15 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://archive.today/20121210094028/http://www.open.edu/openlearn/education/educational-technology-and-practice/educational-technology/1971-home-experiment-kits |archivedate=10 December 2012 |df=dmy-all }}. Retrieved on 28 July 2012.</ref>

Pentz appeared in various [[BBC]] television programmes himself, for example talking to a cat breeder about genetics,<ref>Video clip from the Open University Archive on OpenLearn, The Open University {{cite web |url=http://www.open.edu/openlearn/education/educational-technology-and-practice/educational-technology/1971-early-success |title=1971 - Early success - OpenLearn - Open University |accessdate=2012-06-15 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://archive.today/20121212112511/http://www.open.edu/openlearn/education/educational-technology-and-practice/educational-technology/1971-early-success |archivedate=12 December 2012 |df=dmy-all }}. Retrieved on 28 July 2012.</ref> or demonstrating, with the use of a huge pendulum bob suspended from the dome of St. Paul's Cathedral in London, that the plane in which the pendulum swung actually rotated relative to the cathedral, because of the daily rotation of the Earth.<ref>Picture from the Open University Archive on OpenLearn, The Open University [http://openlearn.open.ac.uk/mod/oucontent/view.php?id=398508&section=4#back_longdesc_id2943245]{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}. Retrieved on 28 July 2012.</ref>

Having built on Pentz's work in establishing science education by distance teaching, the OU's Science Faculty today supports a large proportion of all the part-time science degree studies in the UK: as of 2012, there are about 48,000 (mainly UK-based) students studying OU undergraduate and postgraduate science modules.<ref>'About the faculty', Faculty of Science, The Open University [http://www8.open.ac.uk/science/main/about-the-faculty]. Retrieved 28 July 2012.</ref> Pentz's passion to inform and his belief that science could be taught to anyone who wanted to learn it also inspired many distance educators in other countries and continents to follow his example.<ref name="Durham">{{Cite web |date=1997-11-14 |title=First chance for many, last chance for Earth |url=https://www.timeshighereducation.com/news/first-chance-for-many-last-chance-for-earth/104595.article |access-date=2026-08-28 |website=Times Higher Education (THE) |language=en}}</ref>

==Peace work==
In Pentz's obituary,<ref name="Dalyell"/> Labour politician [[Tam Dalyell]] wrote: "[...] ''no activist bestowed greater scientific respectability on, or devoted more energy to, the crusade against [[nuclear weapon]]s than did Pentz. No big anti-nuclear weapons demonstration in the 1980s was complete without Pentz's large, lumberjacketed presence, leading a march or gracing a platform.''" As an opponent of [[nuclear deterrence]] and of [[NATO]]'s doctrine of flexible response, Pentz believed that a [[nuclear war]] could not in any way remain limited, and would inevitably lead to widespread destruction.<ref name="Pentz">{{cite news | authorlink=Mike Pentz | last=Pentz | first=Mike | title=Das nukleare Wettrüsten – eine neue Initiative ist jetzt dringend notwendig | url=http://www.wissenschaft-und-frieden.de/seite.php?artikelID=0576 | newspaper=Wissenschaft & Frieden, 1984-2 (in German) | accessdate=17 June 2014 | archive-date=19 July 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130719101200/http://www.wissenschaft-und-frieden.de/seite.php?artikelID=0576 | url-status=dead }}</ref> Consequently, Pentz became a vocal activist for [[nuclear disarmament]], joining many significant peace marches of the 1970s and 1980s.
<ref name="Hertfordshire Mercury">"500 at Hertfordshire Peace Festival", Hertfordshire Mercury, 20 May 1983 [http://www.hertfordshiremercury.co.uk/Whats-On-Leisure/500-at-Hertfordshire-peace-festival.htm]{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}. Retrieved 17 June 2014.</ref>

Pentz never sought to conceal controversial affiliations:<ref name="Lewis">{{Cite web |date=1995-06-11 |title=OBITUARY:Professor Mike Pentz |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/obituary-professor-mike-pentz-1586106.html |access-date=2026-08-28 |website=The Independent |language=en}}</ref> he was, for example, a sponsor of the British arm of the leading [[Soviet]] front body, the [[World Peace Council]] (WPC). In May 1984, he went to Moscow at the invitation of the official [[Soviet Peace Committee]] to establish links with the [[Kremlin]]'s "Scientific Research Council on Problems of Peace and Disarmament".<ref name="Lewis"/>

==Legacy==
The [[Open University]] named a building on its campus in [[Milton Keynes]] after Pentz.<ref>'Walton Hall Campus Map', Estates, The Open University [http://www.open.ac.uk/courses/Courses/media/Courses/High%20level%20pages/Contact%20us/wh-campus.png]. Retrieved 7 May 2014.</ref>

==Publications==
* Pentz, Michael J., ''Towards a final abyss? The state of the nuclear arms race''. [[J.D. Bernal]] Peace Library, 1981, 16 pp. ASIN B0007AWP4M.
* Pentz, Michael J., ''Accelerator research at CERN 1956–1967'', CERN 1967, Volume 68, Issue 9 of CERN (Series), 22 pp. 
* Pentz, Michael J., ''British Peace Committee, The nuclear arms race: new dangers, new possibilities of disarmament'', 1976. {{ISBN|0950518204}}, {{ISBN|978-0950518206}}.
* Mike Pentz, Milo Shott, Francis Aprahamian (editor), ''Handling Experimental Data''. [[Open University Press]], 1988, 96 pp. {{ISBN|9780335158249}}.
